sections.title: Two families of vowels
sections.content: The vowels you just met split into two families — back (a, á, o, ó, u, ú) and front (e, é, i, í, ö, ő, ü, ű) — and every Hungarian word belongs to one family or the other, decided by its own vowels. This matters because Hungarian builds words by adding endings, and most endings come in two or three matching versions: one for back-vowel words, one for front-vowel words. You haven't learned any endings yet, so there's nothing to memorise here — just start listening for which family a word belongs to. You'll see this pattern again and again from here on.

sections.title: A preview: one ending, three shapes

sections.content: Don't worry about what that ending means yet — that comes later. For now, just notice: asztal has back vowels, so its ending is -ok; szék has front unrounded vowels, so its ending is -ek; sör has front rounded vowels, so its ending is -ök. Once you know a word's vowel family, you already know which version of an ending it wants — Hungarian speakers do this by ear, without thinking, the way an English speaker's ear rejects "a apple" without a rule to point to.
